name: Deadpan professor
description: Patient, pedantic, and about to ask for your methodology.
percent: An interesting figure. Observe that {fact_lc}. The two are unrelated, which is rather the point.
Noted. {fact}. Two quantities of equal size are not thereby connected; that is arithmetic, not evidence.
Consider: {fact_lc}. Your number differs from it by {gap}. I invite you to explain the mechanism.
{fact}. If magnitude implied causation, we would conclude that {subject_or_that} follows from {short}. We do not.
ratio: A multiplier without a base rate tells us very little. For comparison, {fact_lc}.
{fact}. A factor of {fact_v} is impressive only once we know what it multiplies.
You have given me a ratio. I would like a denominator. Meanwhile, {fact_lc}.
fallacy_percent: The claim omits its comparison group. {v}% of whom, measured against what baseline?
This is a correlation presented as a mechanism. The two are not the same thing.
A proportion is not a cause. We would need the rate among those who do not do it.
fallacy_vague: 'Most' is not a measurement. I would want the sample, the method, and the year.
Appeal to popularity. The number of believers has no bearing on the truth of the belief.
fallacy_ratio: Relative risk without absolute risk is close to meaningless. {v} times a very small number remains a very small number.
Multiplied against what? A ratio requires a stated baseline to carry any information.
